meta.title: A Quiet Skipper
meta.skill_frame: Literary text: judge what a man can do from what he does, not from what his crew says about him.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.6, 5.1 and 5.4 over the three parts (120, 104 and 114 words). The load is a letter's opinion held against a sequence of small acts on a bridge, so the reader tracks two kinds of evidence at once.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Joseph Conrad's novel Typhoon (1902), public domain in the United States.
source.attribution: Conrad, Joseph. Typhoon (1902). Project Gutenberg ebook 1142. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1142 (accessed 2026-11-12).
source.adaptation: Cut the letter to its four opinions, removed the dialect and the long comic asides, and kept the order of the afternoon: swell, glass, bags. No fact was added.
source.survey: A mate's letter about a captain nobody credits, set against the captain's own reading of the weather. Chosen over a storm climax because the judgement can be made from small acts.
source.avoided: No invented ship's route, cargo figures, or weather readings beyond the fall of the glass.

session.difficulty_basis: an opinion in a letter held against a few quiet acts, with the judgement left to the reader

passage.part_1: Mr. Jukes wrote long letters home about his ship. He told his friend that you could not find a quieter skipper than Captain MacWhirr. You would think, he wrote, that the man had not sense enough to see anything wrong. He does nothing actually foolish, and he gets the ship along without worrying anybody. Outside the routine of duty he does not understand more than half of what you tell him. He never talks. Jukes liked the ship, the Eastern trade, and the easy life of it, and he wrote all this as a joke between friends who had served together. He was not a cruel man, and he did not mean the letter to be read by anyone else.
passage.part_2: That afternoon the air turned thick and the sun poured down a pale, leaden heat. The Chinese passengers lay flat about the decks with their eyes shut. Jukes, sewing canvas on the bridge, said aloud that he wondered where the heavy swell came from. MacWhirr answered from his own side of the bridge without looking up. North-east, he said, and told Jukes there was dirty weather about. Then he told him to go and look at the glass. Jukes went into the chart-room. When he came out, his face had changed, and he stood holding the rail and staring ahead without speaking.
passage.part_3: The barometer had fallen a long way, and Jukes said they were going to catch it this time. MacWhirr did not argue about the glass. He looked at the passengers lying on the deck, and at the men who were too sick to move, and he asked what had become of the canvas bags made on the last trip. Jukes said they were worn out. MacWhirr said that more than half of them had gone overboard, if the truth were known, and then he went to the other end of the bridge. The ship lurched heavily in the long hollows of the sea. By evening the swell ran higher, and the ship was labouring.

items.prompt: How much of what you tell him does Jukes say the captain understands?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Not more than half of it.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Jukes writes that outside the routine of duty the captain does not understand more than half of what you tell him.
tutor_only.tell: Jukes says the captain understands not more than half of what he is told.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.
Name the fact the passage gives, then say what it shows.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the captain understands everything
if_they_say.ask: Read the fraction Jukes gives. How much of what he is told does the captain follow?

items.prompt: Jukes says the captain would not see anything wrong. What does the captain do when the swell rises?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. He names the weather and sends Jukes to the glass before Jukes has worried.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Jukes wonders aloud where the swell comes from, and the captain answers north-east and says there is dirty weather about before telling him to look at the glass.
tutor_only.tell: The captain names the swell and the dirty weather first. He sends Jukes to the glass, and Jukes's face changes.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.
Name the fact the passage gives, then say what it shows.
tutor_only.core_idea: he names the dirty weather and sends Jukes to the glass
accept_ideas: he tells Jukes to check the barometer
he says there is dirty weather before Jukes does
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the captain does nothing
if_they_say.ask: The captain answers Jukes's question about the swell. What does he tell him to do next?

items.prompt: The captain asks what became of the canvas bags and says half went overboard. What does that show he has been doing?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. He has been counting and watching the ship's gear while the crew thought he noticed nothing.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The captain asks about the bags made on the last trip and says more than half went overboard, if the truth were known.
tutor_only.tell: He has been watching the gear and counting it. His crew thought he noticed nothing.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.

tutor_only.core_idea: watching and counting the ship's gear
accept_ideas: keeping an eye on the gear
he noticed the bags were missing

if_they_say.when: the student says he is looking for something to complain about
if_they_say.ask: The bag count is accurate. What does an accurate count require?

items.prompt: Jukes writes that 'you could not find a quieter skipper'. What does that phrase do to the opinion that follows?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. It sounds like praise, and the letter then uses it to mean dull.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The praise opens the letter, and the sentences after it say the captain never talks and understands half of what he hears.
tutor_only.tell: The phrase sounds like praise and turns into an insult. Quiet becomes dull in the next lines.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.

tutor_only.core_idea: it sounds like praise and then turns into an insult
accept_ideas: it is praise that becomes an insult

if_they_say.when: the student says the phrase is plain praise
if_they_say.ask: Read the sentences after it. What does Jukes say the quiet man never does?

partial.when: the student says the phrase shows the captain is gentle
partial.ask: Gentle is a feeling. The letter uses quiet to say the man is empty.

tutor_only.full_idea: it sounds like praise and then turns into an insult

items.prompt: The letter and the afternoon on the bridge give two views of the captain. Which should a reader trust, and why?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The bridge, because his acts show what he noticed before anyone else did.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The letter is about how little the captain says. The afternoon shows him reading the swell and the glass first and counting the ship's gear.
tutor_only.tell: Trust the bridge. The letter measures talk, and the acts measure seamanship.
help: The sentence about this sits in the passage. Read it again.
Name the fact the passage gives, then say what it shows.
accept_ideas: what he does on the bridge
the afternoon, since he read the weather first

if_they_say.when: the student says the letter, because a shipmate knows him
if_they_say.ask: A shipmate can still mistake talk for ability. Which evidence is about the work itself?

partial.when: the student says both are true in different ways
partial.ask: One kind of evidence is about talk and one is about the job. Which one answers the question about ability?

tutor_only.full_idea: the bridge, because his acts show what he noticed
